content: Farzana Ismail declared a significant conflict of interest and was excluded from deliberations on moderate complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). She was involved in the evaluation of an extensively drug-resistant (XDR) test prototype by Cepheid, with a research budget of $140,000 in 2020. She also participated in bedaquiline post-marketing surveillance and resistance studies funded by Janssen, with a budget of $300,000, which is ongoing. Additionally, she worked on latent tuberculosis (TB) infection studies in healthcare workers funded by Qiagen, with support for consumables and personnel, which is also ongoing. Blessina Kumar, Nagalineswaran Kumarasamy, Lindiwe Mvusi, Viet Nhung Nguyen, and Sabira Tahseen declared no conflicts of interest. Mark Nicol disclosed that his institution received research grant funding for studies on various novel TB diagnostics, including NAATs such as the BD MAX™ platform, which was of interest to the Guideline Development Group (GDG). Funding sources included the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, NIH, Wellcome Trust, and FIND. His employer, a university, received significant funding (several million USD) from these sources. He also co-holds a pending patent for a novel method to extract and purify DNA from sputum samples, which is unrelated to any commercial TB test and currently has no commercial value. Due to these significant conflicts of interest, he was excluded from discussions on moderate complexity automated NAATs. Leen Rigouts disclosed that her research unit received financial support from FIND for coordinating and participating in a multicenter evaluation of the Genoscholar PZA-LPA test, with partial funding from Nipro. This was deemed a non-significant conflict of interest. Hojoon Sohn, Diana Vakhrusheva, and Francis Varaine declared no conflicts of interest. Ezio Tavora dos Santos Filho coordinated community advisory boards for the PROVE-IT study (TREAT-TB grant funded by the Union/USAID) in Brazil from 2010 to 2015. He is currently following up on the implementation of the Truenat validation study in Brazil and other BRICS countries as an interested party, not as a study team member. He intends to establish systems for community advisory board oversight and protocol analysis in Brazil and partner countries. Due to a perceived significant conflict of interest regarding the Molbio Truenat evaluation, he was excluded from discussions on this topic. Carrie Tudor has been employed by the International Council of Nurses since January 2015. The Council’s TB project received approximately $1 million in funding from the Eli Lilly Foundation (Lilly MDR-TB Partnership) between 2013 and 2019. The current funding period for 2019 was deemed a non-significant conflict of interest. Elisabetta Walters received grants and a scholarship for doctoral research, which included work on the GeneXpert MTB/RIF diagnostic for intrathoracic TB in children. Funding sources included the South African Medical Research Council (2012–2015), a scholarship (2015–2018), the South African National Research Foundation, and FIND. This was deemed a non-significant conflict of interest. Elisa Tagliani participated in the WHO Expert Review Panel for Diagnostics (Round 15), specifically in evaluating the BD MAX platform, for which she received €5940. A unit at San Raffaele received funding from an EDCTP grant (TB-CAPT) to FIND. This was deemed a non-significant conflict of interest for her role as an external reviewer. Danila Zimenkov and Lucilaine Ferrazoli declared no conflicts of interest. Alaine Umubyeyi Nyaruhirira declared no conflicts of interest. Before being invited to join the GDG, potential members are required to submit a completed Declaration of Interests (DOI) form and a curriculum vitae (CV). Additionally, an abbreviated and focused internet search is conducted to identify any public controversies or interests that may compromise the individual’s objectivity. The steering committee evaluates the CV, DOI, and internet findings to determine if conflicts of interest (COI) exist and whether they require a management plan. COI management follows WHO guidelines for DOI for experts, including consultations with the WHO Ethics Team and adherence to the WHO Handbook for guideline development. Both financial and non-financial interests are considered. A significant COI may include intellectual bias, where an individual has repeatedly taken a public position on an issue under review, potentially affecting their objectivity and independence in global policy development. It may also involve research or publications related to the issue under review or financial interests exceeding $5000. Developers of any diagnostic assay are never involved in the policy development process.
